text:
I've had this curiosity for a while now. Lisa is undoubtedly one of the most popular idols in the world, especially internationally, and it seems that no matter what she does, she still has a legion of absolutely dedicated fans. But, the more I think about it, the more I wonder: what is so special about her to reach this level of popularity?
Before you call me a hater, I want to make it clear that I don't think she lacks talent; I recognize that she's a good dancer, but honestly, I don't consider her extraordinary enough to justify all this hype. Even her praised dance performances, like the "lilifilm," aren't that impressive or complex. There are other idols in K-pop that I consider technically superior, more versatile, and capable of demonstrating much more in terms of dance. And many of them don't even receive a fraction of the recognition that Lisa receives.
Regarding rap, I also can't understand what's so impressive about it. She has a recognizable flow and knows how to deliver her parts, but I don't consider her a particularly strong rapper when it comes to writing, technique, and the ability to create her own verses. Vocally, she doesn't stand out either; let's be honest, she's a terrible vocalist. So, if it's not exactly the dancing, rapping, or singing that makes her so special, what is it?
And then there's all the talk about her charisma and stage presence. This is probably the part I understand the least. Personally, I find her performances quite repetitive; often I see the same facial expressions, the same movements, and practically the same approach from one performance to another. I don't feel that ability to surprise or make each performance different. When compared to someone like Jennie, for example, I feel there's a difference in how she manages to convey personality and hold attention on stage. But apparently, I'm one of the few people who sees things this way.
I've also never quite understood the argument that Lisa has an extremely captivating personality. I'm not saying she's an unpleasant person, obviously, but, at least based on the public content I've seen, I've never found anything particularly fascinating about her personality. In interviews, she seems quite reserved, and her answers tend to be simple and superficial. Even so, I constantly see fans talking about her as if she were the most charming person in the world.
What intrigues me is that her popularity seems to go far beyond what her artistic abilities, at least from my perspective, would justify. Even after the release of her solo album, which was very poorly received, she continues to have a huge and extremely dedicated fanbase. And I'm not saying the album should have caused her to lose popularity, but I expected to better understand what sustains this whole phenomenon beyond the name BLACKPINK.
It's one thing to recognize that someone is popular, it's another to understand why. And, in Lisa's case, I feel there's a huge difference between the size of her fame and what I personally can identify as her strengths.
Therefore, I would really like to hear opinions from people who aren't necessarily blind fans or haters. For those who consider Lisa one of the most charismatic and fascinating K-pop artists, what do you see in her that I'm not seeing? What truly distinguishes her from other idols?
label: negative

I go to charity galas every year when my company is a sponsor. We drink, listen to musical performances (often unrelated to the theme), socialize, and just generally have a good time. Sure, there will be a couple 10-minute speeches in the middle talking about the importance of the cause and encouraging further donations, but other than that, it’s just a very expensive social event. The whole idea behind charity galas is that if rich people make big donations to a charity, then they’ll be rewarded with a big party. That’s just how these things work.
Rarely has it been more evident that kpop fans are mostly children with no life experience than when they were losing their minds over last year’s W Korea breast cancer event. It was obvious that none of them had actually been to a corporate fundraiser before because they went into mass psychosis over attendees acting like they were at a party. That’s what a gala is! That’s the normal and expected behavior at this type of event.
Yet people went so insane that it completely took over kpop discourse for weeks and gave us some of the most unhinged takes I’ve ever seen, like shaming Karina’s dress that didn’t completely hide the fact that she has boobs for being “insensitive” to breast cancer survivors, or accusing Taehyung of being a pedophile because he hugged a woman who is literally older than him.
I hoped that a drama so obviously immature and contrived would lead some of the smarter kpop fans to start thinking more critically about the hysteria that so often sweeps through kpop communities and being more careful about perpetuating it, but alas, kpop fans are just as insane now as they were a year ago, if not more so. Still, it’s hard for me to think of a more overblown “scandal” in recent kpop history, given there wasn’t even a kernel of justification for the reactions to this one.

Was there something else that happened that I'm unaware of? Are there specific things he actually did that explain why people still have such a strong negative opinion of him, or is a lot of it just the result of everything surrounding his departure from SKZ and the rumors that followed?
I'm not trying to defend him or start an argument about whether people should like him. I'm genuinely asking because I've never really understood this whole story, and I feel like I might have missed a major part of it.
I'd especially like to know about documented things he actually did, rather than fandom rumors, assumptions about why he left SKZ, or things that have just been repeated so many times that people treat them as fact.

text:
I have been thinking about JYP’s recent comments about FANOMENON and the way he explained the involvement of HYBE, SM, YG and JYP.
Is FANOMENON mainly an investment in the future of K-pop, or is it also a strategic investment by the Big 4 in themselves?
His argument is that the representative artists of these four companies could earn 2–3 times more if they held their own concerts instead of participating in FANOMENON. So, according to him, the companies are giving up a significant amount of short-term revenue because they believe the event can benefit Korea, K-pop and other related industries in the long term.
On the surface, this sounds reasonable. But it also raises another question:
Are the Big 4 really sacrificing money for the benefit of the wider K-pop industry, or are they giving up short-term revenue to invest in an ecosystem that they themselves will control and benefit from?
The distinction is important because these companies are not simply providing artists for an event organised by someone else. They have come together to establish the entity behind FANOMENON, with equal capital contributions and equal voting rights. If the event becomes a successful, recurring global festival, the same companies that are making the short-term sacrifice will also be in a position to benefit from its future growth.
This does not necessarily mean that the project is bad or that their intentions are insincere. However, I am not sure if it should be framed only as a sacrifice for the benefit of Korea or the wider music industry.
There is also the larger question of how much FANOMENON will actually benefit the K-pop industry as a whole.
The event is being presented as something broader than a concert. It is supposed to promote K-pop and K-culture, attract tourism, create opportunities for other industries and possibly develop a larger fandom-related ecosystem. JYP has also spoken about K-pop needing a new system or platform to move into its next stage.
But if FANOMENON becomes the major K-pop festival, could it also concentrate even more attention around the companies that already dominate the industry?
Will smaller and mid-sized agencies genuinely benefit from the exposure? Will their artists be able to use the event to reach international audiences? Or will most of the attention and revenue still go to the biggest artists, while everyone else becomes part of the wider ecosystem around them?
The government has said that artists from the four major agencies will be limited to 30% of the lineup so that artists from smaller Korean agencies can also participate. If this is implemented properly, it could help make the event more representative of the wider industry. But participation alone does not necessarily mean that the benefits will be distributed equally.
There is also a difference between the four companies in terms of the artists they bring and the level of demand those artists have.
BTS is an obvious example. BTS is not only the biggest act in K-pop. Their touring demand exists on a scale that is arguably beyond the usual K-pop market. If HYBE is giving up a BTS stadium concert or tour date for FANOMENON, the opportunity cost could be very different from what another company gives up by having one of its artists participate.
This is not meant to turn the discussion into a BTS comparison or a “BTS is better than everyone else” argument. The point is that when JYP says the representative artists of the four companies could earn 2–3 times more through individual concerts, we cannot assume that the opportunity cost is equal for HYBE, SM, YG and JYP.
The four companies are also not equivalent in terms of their artists, their touring markets or the amount of demand they can generate individually.
So, maybe FANOMENON really is a long-term investment in the Korean entertainment industry. Maybe the four companies genuinely believe that creating a shared platform will generate more value for K-pop and K-culture than simply maximising their individual concert revenue.
But if FANOMENON succeeds, who will ultimately capture that value?
It is possible that the event will benefit Korea, the wider K-pop industry and the four companies at the same time. These things are not mutually exclusive. However, I am not sure if the participation of the Big 4 should automatically be presented as a sacrifice made mainly for everyone else’s benefit.
Nothing is actually confirmed at this stage. I am basing this only on the few times JYP has spoken about FANOMENON and on the reports published by Korean media. The business model, revenue distribution, artist participation and the actual benefits for smaller agencies have not been fully disclosed yet.
So this is not a claim about what the four companies are definitely planning. It is more about questioning the logic behind the project based on the limited information currently available.
label: neutral
note: pre-labelled; evidence: balanced business analysis: 'This does not necessarily mean that the project is bad', 'These things are not mutually exclusive', 'this is not a claim about what the four companies are definitely planning'; mostly open questions

text:
Im okay with loving some artists. 100 percent. You don’t love them like an ordinary person in your life, you love what they represent. This whole condemning of feelings for people you don’t know will keep you from enjoying novels, movies, concerts, almost all entertainment. Who wants to watch a movie if you feel nothing for the characters? Read a novel? This doesn’t mean if you meet them you won’t feel love, but it’s just an exploration of feelings, If you are a teen or early twenties of course it will be intense. So many things are. It’s not going to be transactional, you don’t “get” love back. But it will be a valuable education in how you handle uncomfortable or new feelings. Or even very pleasant ones not in your control. I think mostly you have to wait for them to go away, if that’s what you want.
Fans define too much as parasocial when they dislike someone’s behavior. It’s not a psychopathy. It’s just feelings for someone you don’t know. I can’t imagine anything more normal. Sometimes people are acting out other things, experimenting with confrontation, finding out their values, by using idols as a vehicle. Going to a concert and feeling love and gratitude to a performer who makes you happy. There is a shared experience that idols have who love their fans. Why does nobody call their behavior aberrant? Some don’t believe they love their fans, think it’s just an act. But if they don’t gaf about you because they don’t know you personally, what a horrible job it would be, performing for the equivalent of a bunch of rocks.
If you feel you’ve gone too far, maybe that’s just learning your boundaries which is good. As for putting people on a pedestal, that’s not love, not even parasocial love. Do you put your friends, relatives, romantic partners on pedestals? I hope not.
I think this will happen for your entire life. Crushing on a movie character or star. Feeling warm towards barista or fellow student you don’t know. A famous or not so famous musician making you happy when you see or hear him play. We have all kinds of feelings for people we will never really know. Feelings are some of the least possible things to control. But it’s just human. We aren’t robots. We are connection seeking beings.

text:

Jennie has her identity and established I think way before being in Blackpink. Rosé wants to sing, and she also knows what she is as an artist and what her sound is. Yves (ex-LOONA) released an EP called "LOOP" and I personally love the project because it became a transition from being a loona member to a soloist. Although her sound still connects to loona, she's starting to establish her sound and identity from that EP and the following ones. And with releases such as "I Did", "Soft Error" and now "Nail", I can tell what Yves wants her music to sound like, and she's passionate about it.
In comparison to Lisa, I don't really know how I can separate her from the group she has been in for a whole decade. Her single "Lalisa" was probably a good start, but her other single "Money" felt like a flexing song about money. There's nothing wrong with that but I want to listen and hear her sing who she actually is, because five alter egos are too much. If Lisa actually went to release an EP instead of a full album, I think she could pull off the alter ego concept she's trying to execute. Like each EP represents each alter ego, until she can make a body of work that not just shows who she is but also uses those EPs as a blueprint for establishing her sound.
I'm not really a Blackpink fan and with the recent events about their 10th year anniversary, and Lisa's EP coming up in a few weeks, i don't know what direction she's going with.

I always thought their music just wasn't for me or maybe I just don't like boy bands and to be honest that could still be true. But I recently heard someone talk about the concept of a point of reference and when I applied that logic to my own music taste everything just became clear.
I listen to a lot of alt rnb/rap collectives on a daily basis like Brockhampton, 99 Neighbors, Sad Night Dynamite and Weston Estate to name a few. Because they are constantly in my rotation they naturally become my absolute baseline/point of reference whenever I hear anything even remotely similar.
Whenever a Kpop boy group attempts a hip hop or rnb track to me it just sounds flat. The vocal delivery is just awful in most popular hip hop tracks. The biggest missing piece is the attitude. They fundamentally lack the raw attitude required to pull those genres off and that's why they sound so unoriginal or flat. My brain unknowingly compares the two and they fail miserably in comparison. This is probably the strongest reason and it became especially clear after listening to Lngshot or Cortis because you can say anything about their music but their vocal delivery and attitude is just on point.
With girl groups I simply don't have that same point of reference. I have never listened to any Western girl group music before except for Work by Fifth Harmony and that's it. Because my brain doesn't have that strict baseline or point of reference to instantly compare them against, their music naturally feels fresh and interesting to me. I'm not unknowingly setting them up to fail unlike with boy groups.. so, I can just enjoy the music for exactly what it is. That being said, I do think the music videos for girl groups are just objectively better and more original and unique in comparison.
I do realize my bias and maybe I just haven't explored boy groups enough and I'm just making a generalized statement based on it. Feel free to give your thoughts or just give me song recs and I can give you my honest thoughts and rating.
label: negative
note: pre-labelled; evidence: about boy groups: 'it just sounds flat', 'The vocal delivery is just awful', 'they fail miserably in comparison'; praise for girl groups and LNGSHOT/CORTIS is secondary

text:
The boycott also worked because it hit BlockBerry at exactly the right moment: the company had already spent a ton of money on songs, recordings, photography, four days of location shooting for the MV, and everything else planned for promotion. The albums had probably already been printed and were ready to ship. And the boycott KILLED any chance the company had of making that money back. BlockBerry was in the hole for hundreds of thousands of dollars, maybe more, and they lost it all. The never-ending legal fees simply filled in the grave.
THAT’S how you do a boycott: hit ‘em where and when it hurts.
Now, four years later, boycotting isn’t wrong, but it doesn’t really matter either. The members are safely long gone - their contracts both terminated and expired, the company is dead (or at worst a shambling zombie entity that can no longer harm the LOONA members), and any revenue generated by streaming is minuscule. Fighting over it is not worth the effort now.

text:
2017 was a very weird year to debut, it was a transitional period, concept-wise and marketing-wise, especially for GGs. The mid-2010s were boy-group dominated to a large degree.
Also, I stand by the fact that at a time when groups were getting attention from outside of Korea as well, all the post-IOI groups had way too many members.

Pristin had some hype but not as much as people say they had. It's the same for groups like CLC and Loona, to some extent, who, if you didn't know anything about K-pop, you would think were SNSD reborn just by looking online. text:
Bragging Songs
What inspired this rant is someone calling me a hypocrite for liking Iconic by Mistake by Katsseralit over Sugar Honey Ice Tea by Babymonster when they are both tracks about bragging. Flexing your wealth, saying you don't care about the haters, you know?
And while that was just some butt hurt stan hearing an opinion they don't like. It really got me thinking"What makes a good bragging song?" Well, most likely what makes any song good, good lyrics, or at least catchy lyrics. They are a butt ton of these songs with varying degrees of quality. A bragging song with bad writing just comes across a cliche and blends in with the other songs saying your the best.
Bringing IBM and SHIT as examples. While I have my problems with both I think IBM for the most part has better lyrics. While there are some lyrics I like such as"Never off duty, Taking a beating, I keep on cheesing, Looks are deceiving""Honestly, are you okay?" And some I don't like"Heart, heart it, Heart it harder, Here, heart is like a verb, Come heal it where it hurts" For the most part and especially considering the context that all three of these groups went through massive hate trains. I think it does a good job conveying its message. It could be better, but it's not bad.
For SHIT, lyrics like"I'm the sugar honey ice tea and you know it, Ain't no other baddie like me, yeah, you know it" The songs just seem to be relying hard on the title. Which while a clever one, can't save the song. But even then the song wouldn't be that bad in a vacuum. But it's also the fact that bragging songs are the only songs YG seems to know how to make. Which while that's a whole other can of worms, definitely does sour my enjoyment.
So, what are some examples of bragging songs done right? Immediately XG's Gala comes to mind. I know some people consider XG kpop but whatever. Lyrics like"I could dress casually, naturally, anything becomes a masterpiece""Only ELLE I know is the mag', what's the issue?" It's simply perfection. Also Illit's It's Me comes to mind. I also know people have mixed views on the song but also whatever. Lyrics like"Prada? I'm more expensive, I can't be replaced""Just sittin' 'round like tortilla Why?" They are extremely silly and I really like them. And the hook of the song"Who's your bias? I'm your bias!" Is what I mean by not good lyrics but catchy lyrics. While the hook is not bad nor mind blowing, it does its job by sticking in your brain.

text:
There's nothing wrong with trying different things, but at the end of the day, group activities and music careers aren't personal hobbies. The goal is to establish a clear image in the market and build a dedicated fanbase around it. To do that, a group needs something that sets them apart from everyone else and then consistently reinforces it over time.
That distinction doesn't necessarily have to come from the music itself. It can be a visual identity, an overall aesthetic, or simply the vibe the group gives off. Take ILLIT, for example. Their music varies quite a bit from release to release, but the group's image and the members' overall appeal remain remarkably consistent, which is why it works. The same applies to NMIXX. They experiment with all kinds of genres, yet people still associate them with strong vocal and performance skills as well as their identity of blending different musical styles.
In the end, whether it's achieved through music or through non-musical elements, groups have to convince the public with a distinct and recognizable identity. There's really no getting around that.

text:
Ace = top-tier in a skill, this is the person who performs a skill at the highest level to the point where if they were competing against others they would be almost impossible to beat (like an Ace in a deck of cards, it’s usually the highest card)
Ex. BoA is an ace dancer, Bobby (iKON) is an ace rapper, Baekhyun (EXO) is an ace singer
All-rounder = someone who excels at most or every skill. Every idol for the most part is proficient at every basic skill (vocals, dancing, stage presence, etc.). An all-rounder is above average (compared to other idols not compared to you or me) at all skills.
Ex. Han Jisung from Stray Kids is an above average dancer, vocalist, rapper, songwriter, producer, and performer… he can do every skill and he can do each one as well as or better than the average idol
Some idols are both (ex. Han is an all-rounder and an ace rapper/producer) but not every ace is an all-rounder and not every all-rounder is an ace. And many fans overestimate how many idols fit into both categories. Aces are rarer than all-rounders. Every group does not have aces/all-rounders, and there’s very few (like count on less than one hand) where all the members are truly all-rounders, contrary to what fans may believe.
